messages.body_plain:
Hello,

As a new unmarked user...I am trying to understand something about the hmat file that is created as part of the Temporary Emigration model described in Chandler (2015) vignette "Modeling variation in abundance using capture-recapture data"

I see the issue when playing with the alder flycatcher data and code described in the vignette as well as my own data.

Specifically, sites with no detections and those with detections seem to match up with the raw data from the first survey, but there is no variation among the surveys, even when the raw data suggest there should be...for example, in the alder flycatcher data: his1_05 shows two birds with detection histories in the first seven columns (under 011 and 111), but the raw data suggest that during the second survey, there was a third bird detected with a history of 101, but that is not shown in the next 7 columns of the hmat file where each site seems to have the same detection histories during all three surveys.

Does anyone know if this is a problem, and if so, how to fix it.  It seems that each of three sets of 7 columns represent the detection histories for each of the three surveys and therefore should reflect that survey.
We have tried playing around with the cbind function that is responsible for creation of the hmat table to no avail.

Thanks so much for any thoughts on this.

Lesley Bulluck

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am fairly new to the use of unmarked for the colext models, so bare with me if this is very basic.
Although I have followed some similar post, cannot seem to find what I need.

I selected the following best model from  selection procedure (same results in Presence and in Unmarked):

mbest <- colext(psiformula= ~ Forest  , gammaformula = ~year-1, epsilonformula = ~ year-1+ ~ NP + ~Properties, pformula = ~ year-1 + ~ Under, data =bm, method ="BFGS")

I want to be able to plot covariates fitted for epsilon separately (i.e. NP and Properties).   These were z-transformed.

I have been able to plot yearly epsilon estimates by leaving NP and Properties = 0.

ndext1<- data.frame(year=c("01","02","03"), NP =0, Properties = 0 )
E.ext1 <- predict(mbest, type="ext", newdata=ndext1).

But no such luck selecting for NP or Properties separately.

I have tried:

ndext2<- data.frame(year =0, NP = seq(-1.5152, 4.2756, length = 145), Properties = 0)  # seq are the min and max values of the covariate
E.ext2 <- predict(mbest, type="ext", newdata=ndext2)
I get the follwowing error:
Error: ncol(coefficients) == length(obj@estimates) is not TRUE

When I try:
ndext2<- data.frame( NP = seq(-1.5152, 4.2756, length = 145)) # I use 145 because this is my number of sample units
E.ext2 <- predict(mbest, type="ext", newdata=ndext2)

I get:  Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : object 'Properties' not found

So then I try:
ndext2<- data.frame(NP = seq(-1.5152, 4.2756, length = 145), Properties =0)
E.ext2 <- predict(mbest, type="ext", newdata=ndext2)

and I get:  Error in `[[<-.data.frame`(`*tmp*`, i, value = c(1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L, 1L,  :
  replacement has 580 rows, data has 145

An additional problem is that these covariates were z-transformed.  Therefore my question is if there is a way to convert them back for plotting with values that make more sense.

Any suggestions are more than welcomed.  THANKS!!!

messages.body_plain:
WORKSHOP
Modelling the distribution of species and communities accounting for detection using R and BUGS/JAGS

Instructors:    Gurutzeta Guillera Arroita, José Lahoz-Monfort (University of Melbourne)
& Marc Kéry (Swiss Ornithological Institute)

Date:               11–15 January 2016

Venue:            Mediterranean Institute for Advanced Studies (IMEDEA, CSIC-UIB),
Esporles (Mallorca), Spain

Computers:    Bring your own laptop with latest R, JAGS and WinBUGS or OpenBUGS

Costs:              500 Euro (includes course materials and snacks/coffee/tea)

Species distribution modelling has become a fundamental tool in ecology and conservation, where it underpins many applications. However, species distribution models are not always fit for purpose. How informative or useful a model is strongly depends on the type of question and also on the type of data used to fit the model. This course gives a critical overview of existing techniques for species distribution modelling for single species as well as for entire communities. We start by presenting methods for presence-only, presence-background and presence-absence data, discussing their strengths and limitations. We then introduce a key class of models for the analysis of species distributions that explicitly accounts for the observation (or measurement error) process that underlies all species distribution data. This framework, the focus of the course, includes site-occupancy models (MacKenzie et al. 2002, 2003; Tyre et al. 2003) and extensions for modelling abundance, range dynamics and communities. The course partly follows the brand-new book “Applied hierarchical modeling in ecology” (Academic Press, 2015) by Kéry & Royle. Model fitting is shown using the Bayesian BUGS software and the R package unmarked. Importantly, the course showcases the practical model fitting of community, or multi-species, occupancy models highlighted in recent papers such as Iknayan et al. (TREE, 2014) and Mihaljevic et al. (Ecology, 2015).

Course modules include the following:

·         Introduction to species distribution modelling: questions/applications, theory and data types

·         Overview of presence-only, presence-background and presence-absence methods

·         Static (= single-season) occupancy-detection models in R and BUGS

·         Dynamic (= multi-season) occupancy-detection models in R and BUGS

·         Models for communities, including co-occurrence models

·         Overview of extensions and related models, e.g. abundance models, spatial autocorrelation, and integrated models (combining data types)

In addition, the course will start with an introduction to Bayesian statistical modelling using BUGS software and likelihood-based estimation using R. In this applied workshop about 80% of the time is spent on lecturing and the remainder on solving exercises. No previous experience with program WinBUGS, or Bayesian statistics, is assumed. However, a good working knowledge in R programming and of modern regression methods (e.g. generalised linear models) is required.

Please send your application to Guru (ggui...@unimelb.edu.au), describing your background and knowledge in statistical modelling, R and WinBUGS/OpenBUGS/JAGS, by 1 December 2015 at the latest. Workshop invitations will be sent out before 4 December 2015.

Travel information: Esporles is a village at about 14 km north of Palma, the capital of Mallorca. Several companies offer low-cost flights to Mallorca from nearly every European capital. There are regular buses between Palma and Esporles (approx. 35min journey, about 3 € return). Information about accommodation options and a detailed course schedule will be sent out with the workshop invitations.

Travis

Hi everyone,

I just saw a few talks by the folks giving this workshop. Looks like really interesting stuff so though i would send the info around in case anyone is interested:

On 27-30 October 2015 Duke Environmental Leadership program in collaboration with the University of St Andrews will offer a workshop on spatial modelling methods for distance sampling line transect data.

The workshop will cover: the basics of organizing survey data in ArcGIS using the MGET toolbox, developed at the Marine Geospatial Ecology Lab, Duke; followed by building and evaluating spatially explicit models of abundance (using environmental predictors) in R, using packages developed at the Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling, St Andrews. The aim will be to demonstrate an end-to-end workflow for spatial modelling of distance sampling data, and illustrate the underlying theory behind both spatial modelling using generalized additive models and distance sampling (we will focus on the "density surface modelling" approach).

The course is intended for graduate students/postdocs/faculty in applied ecology, government/industry scientists and wildlife managers interested in developing spatially explicit models of abundance. Prior knowledge of R and ArcGIS will be highly advantageous, as is a quantitative background.

The course will be taught by David L Miller (St Andrews), Jason J Roberts (Duke) and Eric Rexstad (St Andrews), at the Duke campus in Durham, NC.

The deadline for registration is 12 October 2015.

Detailed information on the course content and registration can be found at https://nicholas.duke.edu/del/distance.

messages.subject_clean: Interpretation of detection probabilities from autonomous portable recorders
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I`m having some philosophical interrogations about occupancy using Unmarked, and I would like to know if anyone can help me.

I`m interested in exploring the influence of elevation and forest type over the distribution and the vocal behavior of a rare and endemic bird of Puerto Rico: The Elfin- woods warbler. This is a territorial species with very small territories.

I deployed 2 autonomous portable recorders every 100 meters in elevation (from 95 to 1047 meters) in three different elevational transects. I have 63 sampling points with an average of seven secondary occasions per point (1 to 14 days of sampling at every site). Recorders were programed to record 1 minute every 10 minutes totalizing 144 recordings per day. I used autonomous algorithm to detect the species on the recordings and I found the species in 22 sampling sites . Then I visually scanned all the recordings from all the 22 sampling sites with confirmed species presences and counted the number of times the species vocalized at every site (~ 800 detections at total). Although I can have a lot of detections per day, I`m just coding: 1-detected or 0-not for each day.  So, when the species is present in a site I was able to detect it almost every day. Nevertheless, there is some sites where I wasn`t able to detect the species every day.

The simple occupancy model – psi(.)p(.) gives me:

Psi =0.349 (0.06)

p=0.76(0.032)

My main questions are:

1)   How can I interpret p (detection probability) in this case? I believe that detection probabilities are not so linked with the sampling process anymore. I`m guessing that detection probability here is only the probability that a bird sing during the recordings. In that case, I think that I don`t have any variables to model the detection probability ( maybe Julian days).

2)   I`m guessing that the variation on the number of detection in each sites is related with the position of the recorder along the bird territory. Maybe sites with a lot of detections are at the center of the bird`s territories while sites with low number of detections are at the border of the bird`s territories. So, if this makes sense, I should opt for the multi-state occupancy models, right?. But again, I don`t know how to interpret detection probabilities in this scenario.

Any commentaries will be appreciated!

Sorry for the long email!

Best regards

Marconi

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marconi,

1)  The way you've summarized the data means that p is the probability of ever detecting the species during the 144 recordings in a day.

2)  You might look into multi-scale occupancy models (in PRESENCE or BUGS) to calculate the probabilities of occupancy (site-level), availability (day-level), and detection (minute-level).  Availability would presumably be higher for sites that are closer to a bird's territory.  You might have to thin the minute-level data to create reasonably independent samples, but this is somewhat similar to GPS collar data where animal locations are too close in time to consider independent.  If you wanted to use the full data set you'd have to go with some more complex models that are certainly out there, but not as well understood (or easy to implement).

Here is paper I like, that can also point you to additional citations:

Mordecai, R.S., Mattsson, B.J., Tzilkowski, C.J. & Cooper, R.J. (2011) Addressing challenges when studying mobile or episodic species: hierarchical Bayes estimation of occupancy and use. Journal of Applied Ecology, 48, 56-66.

 What is the difference between a site and a point count location?  If a site has 2 point count locations in it and you treat them as independent then why not just call this "2 sites"?

 If the variation among sites is only due to fixed effects like regression variables then you can model that directly using any of the functions in unmarked.
 If you're interested in modeling random site effects to account for the grouping of non-independent points within a site, then you probably have to use BUGS to fit such models (examples of this are given in the forthcoming book Applied Hierarchical Models by Marc Kery and myself).

regards
andy

Please consider adding a way to account for this in future versions of unmarked because it's value would be greatly improved for many researchers.

Don

messages.body_plain:
Hi Don,

What are the general objectives of the study?  How are you defining sites/surveys, etc.?  What kind of detection data do you have?  It is certainly best to design your sampling with the intended modeling framework and study objectives in mind.  If it is too late for that, sometimes pragmatic decisions are necessary that require simplification, making or potentially violating some assumptions, or discarding some data.

With 185 sites and 221 point counts, you have a very small proportion of sites with point count replicates.  What is the purpose of the replicates?  Depending on the complexity of your model and the covariates included, your inferences using 221 independent point counts (despite violations of independence) vs. 185 independent point counts (1 per site, with some counts discarded) are not going to be all that different.  You should try fitting both the original data assuming independence and the reduced data with 1 point count per site and report back with what you find.

messages.body_plain:
Well, the problem is that random site effects would need to be integrated out of the likelihood when fitting the models using MLE, and unmarked models are already dealing with integration of latent variables (true occurrence or abundance), so trying to account for additional unstructured variation would be tricky.  A ton of work for little gain, under the types of data scenarios that are most common.  It is certainly not impossible - see the "lme4" package or Program MARK.  But it is not a straightforward problem that can simply be added.  If you really care about multiple dimensions of random effects, a Bayesian approach is usually necessary (as used in Zipkin et al. 2010).

Also, sometimes a little pseudoreplication is not so bad.  By including the replicates as independent points, you could actually have a better representation of the uncertainty for density relationships with covariates.  Un-modeled heterogeneity is the concern, but again, it's just a model!

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

My apologies for what may be a simple answer to this question. I have spent many hours trying to find a solution, to no avail.

I am currently analyzing a dataset of jaguar occupancy across 1442 sites (it's for all of Central America, hence the number of sites). We have a maximum of 6 occasions per site.

I have been able to run standard single-season models in unmarked just fine with these data, and yet when I use unmarkedFrameOccuFP and occuFP I get the error message "Error in pvec * (1 - bvec) : non-conformable arrays." The error message leads me to believe that the data going into unmarkedFrameOccuFP are not of the correct dimension, though I have done many checks to ensure that they are--- plus, the models run in occu just fine. I have cells with missing data, as we were not able to collect 6 surveys in all sites. There are also sites with zero surveys. Perhaps this is a problem for occuFP?

Or maybe I am using incorrect syntax, specifically in the "type" argument, as that appears to be the only difference in preparing data for occu and occuFP.

I have provided my code below. Crossing my fingers and hoping that someone is able to help.

My thanks,
Lisanne Petracca

#set working directory
setwd("I:/Jaguar_Corridor_Single_Occupancy_Analysis/Occupancy")

#import 32 site covariates for 1442 sites
as.data.frame(site_cov<-read.csv("SiteCovariates.csv", header=T, row.names=1))

#import detection history--- composed of 0s, 1s, and 2s--- 2s are certain detections, 1s uncertain
as.data.frame(detect<-read.csv("Jaguar_Max6.csv", header=T, row.names=1))

#Convert dashes to NA for Unmarked
detect[detect=="-"] <-NA
detect<-apply(detect, 2, function(x){as.numeric(as.character(x))})

#import three detection covariates
as.data.frame(effort<-read.csv("Effort_Max6.csv", header=T, row.names=1))
effort[effort=="-"]<-NA
effort<-apply(effort, 2, function(x){as.numeric(as.character(x))})

as.data.frame(year<-read.csv("Year_Max6.csv", header=T, row.names=1))
year[year=="-"]<-NA
year<-apply(year, 2, function(x){as.factor(as.character(x))})

as.data.frame(corridor<-read.csv("Corridor_Max6.csv", header=T, row.names=1))
corridor[corridor=="-"]<-NA
corridor<-apply(corridor, 2, function(x){as.factor(as.character(x))})

#declare that all six occasions are of type III (certain and uncertain detections, accounting for false positives)
type <- as.vector(c(0, 0, 6))

#build OccuFP data frame
Jagmodel<-unmarkedFrameOccuFP(y=detect, siteCovs=site_cov, obsCovs=list(effort=effort, year=year, corridor=corridor), type=type)

#build first model
fm.null <- occuFP(detformula = ~ 1, FPformula = ~ 1, Bformula = ~ 1, stateformula = ~ 1, data = Jagmodel)

Hi Sameer,

Thanks for the kind words, but a lot of other people deserve credit for unmarked.

I'm guessing that your problem is due to the way you coded observer. In unmarked, you do not have to create dummy variables yourself; they will be created automatically from a factor. However, it's fine to do it yourself, but you need to be careful. In your case, I think you only have 2 observers (is that correct?) and so you need to either exclude the intercept or exclude one of the observers from the model. Here is a way to remove the intercept:

occu(~obs + date - 1 ~ grass, data = sinh.sum)

Richard
